lessons.title: Set up Claude and finish your first real work task in one conversation
lessons.summary: Create your Claude account, learn the layout of the app, and complete a genuinely useful work task — preparing for a meeting — in your very first chat.
lessons.goal: Open a Claude account and use your first conversation to turn a vague meeting into a clear agenda with talking points.
lessons.whyItMatters: Most people's first AI conversation is a throwaway — a joke, a trivia question — and they walk away unsure what the tool is actually for. Starting with a real task changes that: you immediately see how Claude handles context, follows instructions, and produces work you can use. Meeting preparation is a perfect first task because everyone has a meeting coming up and the output is easy to judge.
lessons.beforeYouStart: You need an email address to create a free account at claude.ai. No payment details are required for the Free plan.
steps: Go to claude.ai and sign up with your email (or Google account). The Free plan is enough for this whole lesson.

Take 30 seconds to orient yourself: the large text box is where you type, past conversations appear in the sidebar, and the paperclip/plus icon lets you attach files. Paid plans also show a model picker near the input box.
Think of a real meeting you have in the next week — a client call, a team sync, a negotiation, anything.
Copy the prompt below, replace the placeholders in brackets with your real details, and send it.
Read the response critically, as you would a colleague's draft. Notice what it got right and what is generic.
Send one follow-up in the same chat to fix the weakest part — for example: 'Talking point 2 is too vague. My counterpart cares most about cost, so reframe it around budget impact.'
Copy the final agenda somewhere you will actually use it (calendar invite, notes app). You have now done real work with Claude.
lessons.prompt:
I have a meeting coming up and I want to walk in prepared.

Meeting: [WHAT THE MEETING IS, e.g. "30-minute call with a potential client about redesigning their website"]
Who will be there: [PEOPLE AND ROLES]
What I want to get out of it: [YOUR DESIRED OUTCOME]
What I'm worried about: [CONCERNS, OBJECTIONS YOU EXPECT, OR "nothing specific"]

Please give me:
1. A tight agenda for the time available, with minutes per item
2. 3-4 talking points for my main goal, each one sentence
3. The two hardest questions I might get asked, with a suggested one-line answer for each

Keep the whole thing under 300 words so I can review it in two minutes. Base everything only on what I've told you — if something important is missing, ask me instead of guessing.
lessons.explanation: This prompt works because it gives Claude the four things it cannot invent for you: the situation, the people, your goal, and your worries. The numbered output request means you get a structured document rather than a rambling essay, and the 300-word cap forces prioritization. The last line — 'ask me instead of guessing' — is a habit worth building from day one: it tells Claude that missing information should become a question, not an invented detail. Your follow-up message demonstrates the core rhythm of working with Claude: first draft, then refine in the same conversation.
lessons.example:
Input: "Meeting: 30-minute call with the owner of a 12-room boutique hotel about managing their social media. Who: just me and the owner, Maria. Goal: get her to agree to a 3-month trial at 600 EUR/month. Worried about: she thinks her niece can do it for free."

Output: Claude returns a 30-minute agenda (5 min rapport, 10 min her goals and current situation, 10 min your proposal, 5 min next steps), talking points such as "A trial makes this reversible — three months, then we look at the booking numbers together," and hard questions like "Why shouldn't my niece just do this?" with the suggested answer "She absolutely could post photos — what I bring is a posting system tied to your booking calendar, so quiet weeks get promoted before they happen."
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, run the prompt above for a real meeting or call you have this week. Then send at least one follow-up message that sharpens the weakest talking point.
lessons.expectedResult: A one-page agenda with talking points and prepared answers that you would genuinely bring to the meeting — produced and refined in under ten minutes.
commonMistakes: Leaving the placeholders vague ('a meeting with a client') — the less context you give, the more generic the output. Specific inputs are what separate useful answers from filler.
Treating the first response as final. Claude's first draft is a starting point; one or two follow-ups usually double the quality.
Starting a brand-new chat for the follow-up. Stay in the same conversation so Claude keeps all the context you already provided.
lessons.proTip: After the meeting actually happens, return to the same chat and tell Claude how it went. Ask 'What should I do differently next time?' — you'll get a short debrief informed by everything you planned together.

lessons.title: Write prompts that get professional-quality answers on the first try
lessons.summary: Learn the four-part prompt structure — context, role, constraints, format — that turns Claude from a generic chatbot into a reliable colleague.
lessons.goal: Use the context-role-constraints-format structure to write a prompt that produces work you could hand to your boss with minimal edits.
lessons.whyItMatters: The difference between a mediocre AI answer and an excellent one is almost never the model — it's the prompt. People who write 'write me a marketing plan' get boilerplate; people who specify the situation, the perspective, the boundaries, and the shape of the output get drafts that look like a professional wrote them. This one skill multiplies the value of every other lesson in this course.
steps: Pick a real writing or thinking task from your work — something you would otherwise spend 30+ minutes on.
Write the CONTEXT: who you are, what the situation is, who the output is for. Two to four sentences. This is the part most people skip and it matters most.
Add a ROLE when a specific perspective helps: 'Act as an experienced employment lawyer reviewing this for risk' produces a different, sharper answer than no role at all.
Add CONSTRAINTS: length limits, what to include, what to avoid, tone boundaries, and — when facts matter — 'use only the information I give you; if something is missing, say so'.
Specify the FORMAT: a table, numbered list, email draft, bullet summary, or 'exactly three options, each with a one-line rationale'.
Send the prompt, then grade the answer: which of the four parts was too thin? Strengthen that part and resend, comparing the two answers.
Save your best version — you will turn prompts like this into reusable templates in lesson 11.
lessons.prompt:
CONTEXT: I run a small [TYPE OF BUSINESS] with [N] employees. [2-3 SENTENCES ON THE SITUATION — what happened, what you have, who the output is for.]

ROLE: Act as [THE EXPERT YOU'D HIRE FOR THIS, e.g. "a pragmatic operations consultant who has worked with small businesses"].

TASK: [THE ONE THING YOU WANT, e.g. "propose how to handle the scheduling conflicts described above"].

CONSTRAINTS:
- Use only the information I've provided; where you're making an assumption, label it "Assumption:"
- Solutions must cost under [BUDGET] and be doable within [TIMEFRAME]
- Plain language, no jargon or hype

FORMAT: Exactly 3 options. For each: a bold one-line title, a 2-3 sentence description, and one main risk. End with a one-sentence recommendation of which option you'd pick and why.
lessons.explanation: Each section does distinct work. Context grounds the answer in your reality instead of the average of the internet. Role selects which expertise and communication style Claude draws on — 'pragmatic consultant' and 'academic researcher' write very differently. Constraints prevent the two most common failures: answers that ignore your real limits, and confident filler where facts are missing (the 'label your assumptions' line is a lightweight anti-hallucination guardrail). Format determines whether you get something scannable and usable or a wall of text. You won't need all four parts for every message — but when the output matters, running through all four takes 90 seconds and routinely saves a rewrite.
lessons.example:
Weak prompt: "How do I deal with a difficult employee?" — returns generic HR advice you could find anywhere.

Structured prompt: "CONTEXT: I own a 6-person cafe. My best barista, employed 2 years, has arrived 20-40 minutes late five times in the past two weeks. Previously flawless. I want to keep her. ROLE: Act as an experienced small-business HR advisor. TASK: Plan the conversation I should have with her. CONSTRAINTS: I have no HR department; keep it legally cautious but human; use only what I've told you and label assumptions. FORMAT: A 5-step conversation plan, with an example opening sentence for step 1."

Output: A specific, humane conversation plan that opens with concern rather than accusation ("I've noticed the last two weeks have looked different for you, and I wanted to check in before anything else — is everything okay?"), flags the assumption that something changed in her life, and includes a step on agreeing concrete expectations going forward.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, take a task you'd normally ask a colleague for help with. Write it twice: first as a one-line question, then using the full four-part structure. Send both in separate chats and compare the answers side by side.
lessons.expectedResult: The structured version should be visibly more specific, better organized, and closer to usable-as-is. If the two answers look similar, your context section was probably too thin — add detail and try again.
commonMistakes: Writing constraints for the model instead of the work. 'Be accurate and helpful' does nothing; 'under 200 words, no exclamation marks, cite which bullet each claim comes from' changes the output.
Using a role as a magic spell ('act as the world's best marketer') without any context. Role amplifies context; it doesn't replace it.
Cramming five tasks into one prompt. One prompt, one deliverable. Chain follow-ups for the rest.
Forgetting the format section, then spending time reformatting a wall of text you could have received as a table.
lessons.proTip: When you can't articulate what you want, invert the flow: paste your context and write 'Before answering, ask me the 3-5 questions you need to do this well.' Claude's questions will often reveal constraints you didn't know you had.

lessons.title: Rewrite any draft: change the tone, cut the length, keep the facts
lessons.summary: Use Claude as a reliable editor that shortens, polishes, and re-tones your drafts without losing meaning or inventing new claims.
lessons.goal: Take a rough draft you've written and reliably transform it — shorter, clearer, or in a different tone — while keeping every fact intact.
lessons.whyItMatters: Editing your own writing is slow because you're too close to it. Claude excels at the mechanical half of editing — cutting words, smoothing sentences, shifting register from casual to formal or stern to warm — and it does so in seconds. The professional risk is silent fact-drift: an over-eager rewrite that softens '3 missed deadlines' into 'some delays'. This lesson teaches a rewrite prompt with guardrails against exactly that.
steps: Find a real draft: an email you hesitated to send, a paragraph for your website, a report section that's too long.
Decide on ONE primary transformation: shorten, change tone, or improve clarity. Name the target precisely — 'warmer but still firm about the deadline' beats 'make it better'.
Paste the prompt below with your draft and your target. Keep the 'do not change facts' guardrail — it's the most important line.
Read the rewrite next to your original. Check the change log Claude provides: did any number, name, date, or commitment shift?
Refine with follow-ups that adjust one dial at a time: 'Good, now 20% shorter' or 'The second paragraph lost the apology — restore it.'
For important messages, ask for two versions at different intensities and choose, rather than trying to describe the perfect tone in advance.
lessons.prompt:
Rewrite the draft below.

What I want changed: [e.g. "cut it to roughly half the length and make the tone warmer and less bureaucratic — it's going to a long-time client"]
Who will read it: [AUDIENCE]
What must NOT change: every fact, number, date, name, and commitment stays exactly as written. Do not add claims, promises, or details that aren't in my draft. Keep [ANYTHING ELSE TO PRESERVE, e.g. "the apology in the first paragraph"].

Give me:
1. The rewritten text
2. A short change log: what you cut, what you rephrased, and a note if any sentence's meaning may have shifted

Draft:
[PASTE YOUR DRAFT]
lessons.explanation: Naming a single primary transformation keeps the rewrite controlled — asking for 'shorter, friendlier, more professional, and punchier' at once gives Claude license to rewrite everything. The 'must not change' list is the guardrail that makes this safe for real correspondence: tone edits are exactly where facts get accidentally softened or sharpened. The change log turns your review from re-reading two full texts into scanning a short diff — and asking Claude to flag possible meaning shifts recruits it into its own quality control. Follow-ups that move one dial at a time ('20% shorter') converge much faster than repeatedly re-describing the whole goal.
lessons.example:
Input draft (excerpt): "Per my previous email, the invoice #2241 from March 3rd remains unpaid. This is the third reminder. We must insist on immediate payment of the outstanding 1,840 EUR, failing which we will be forced to suspend services."

Target: "Warmer and more personal — this client has paid on time for four years — but keep the suspension warning."

Output: "Hi Thomas, I wanted to flag this personally because it's so unusual for your account. Invoice #2241 (1,840 EUR, from March 3rd) is still open — you've been reliably on time for four years, so I suspect it simply slipped through. Could you take a look this week? I do have to mention that if it stays unpaid we'd eventually need to pause services, which is the last thing either of us wants." Change log notes: kept invoice number, amount, date, and the suspension consequence; replaced 'third reminder' framing with 'unusual for your account' — flagged as a meaning-adjacent change for your review.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, paste a real email or document draft and run the prompt twice with two different targets (e.g. 'half the length' and 'more formal'). Verify against the originals that every number and date survived both rewrites.
lessons.expectedResult: Two clean rewrites in clearly different registers, each with a change log, and zero altered facts. If a fact did change, tighten the 'must not change' list and rerun.
commonMistakes: Asking to 'make it better' with no target. Claude will guess a direction and you'll iterate blindly. Name the audience and the specific change.
Skipping the fact-check. A tone rewrite that turns 'we cannot refund this' into 'we'll see what we can do' has changed your legal position, not just your tone.
Rewriting a draft five times in a row until it loses your voice. If version 3 isn't clearly better than version 2, take version 2 and finish it yourself.
Pasting only a fragment of the draft for context reasons and getting a rewrite that contradicts the parts Claude never saw.
lessons.proTip: To teach Claude your voice, paste two or three past emails you're proud of and say: 'Match the tone and sentence rhythm of these examples when rewriting.' Concrete examples beat any adjective-based tone description.

lessons.title: Turn a 40-page document into a one-page brief you can trust
lessons.summary: Upload a long PDF, contract, or report and get a faithful executive summary — with the guardrails that keep the summary honest.
lessons.goal: Upload a long document to Claude and produce a structured one-page brief that accurately reflects what the document actually says.
lessons.whyItMatters: Long documents are where professional time disappears: 60-page reports read for three usable pages, contracts skimmed and mis-remembered, tender documents nobody fully reads. Claude reads the whole thing in seconds and can summarize at whatever depth you need. The skill worth learning is not 'ask for a summary' — it's asking in a way that forces faithfulness: sourced claims, flagged gaps, and no smoothing-over of what the document leaves unsaid.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have a real document ready (PDF, Word, or plain text). Claude accepts up to 20 files per chat, 30 MB each, on all plans. Avoid uploading documents you're not permitted to share with an external service — check your company's policy for confidential material.
steps: Click the attachment (paperclip/plus) icon in the chat input and upload your document, or drag it into the chat.
Before asking anything, tell Claude who you are and what decision or task the summary feeds. A summary 'for a buyer deciding whether to sign' is a different document than 'for a team meeting update'.
Send the prompt below. The structure (summary, key points, obligations/risks, gaps) fits most business documents; adjust the sections to your document type.
Spot-check before trusting: pick two or three claims from the summary, ask 'Where exactly does the document say this? Quote the passage,' and verify the quotes against the file.
Drill into whatever matters most: 'Expand the termination clause section — what exactly are the notice periods?'
Save the final brief. For recurring document types (contracts, reports), save your prompt too — it becomes a template in lesson 11.
lessons.prompt:
I've uploaded [WHAT THE DOCUMENT IS, e.g. "a 38-page commercial lease agreement"]. I am [YOUR ROLE AND SITUATION, e.g. "the prospective tenant, deciding this week whether to sign"].

Summarize it for that purpose:
1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY — 5 sentences max: what this document is and the most important things it establishes
2. KEY POINTS — the 5-8 points that matter most for my situation, one bullet each
3. OBLIGATIONS AND RISKS — anything that binds me, costs me money, or could hurt me later, each with the section/page it comes from
4. WHAT'S MISSING OR UNCLEAR — things I'd expect a document like this to cover that it doesn't, or clauses that are ambiguous

Rules: use only what the document actually says — never fill gaps with what such documents typically contain. For every point in sections 2 and 3, cite the section or page number. If you're uncertain what a clause means, say so rather than picking an interpretation.
lessons.explanation: Stating your role and decision turns a generic abstract into a targeted brief — Claude weighs a penalty clause very differently for a tenant than for a landlord. The four-section structure separates 'what it says' from 'what it means for you', and section 4 is the one most people never think to ask for: what a document fails to say is often the biggest risk. The rules line does the safety work: requiring citations makes every claim checkable in seconds, banning typical-document filler prevents Claude from 'summarizing' standard clauses that aren't actually in your file, and inviting uncertainty gives it permission to say 'this clause is ambiguous' instead of guessing.
lessons.example:
Input: A 38-page lease PDF, uploaded with the prompt above filled in for a prospective tenant.

Output (excerpt): "OBLIGATIONS AND RISKS: (1) Rent increases annually by CPI + 2%, uncapped — Section 4.3, p.7. (2) You are responsible for ALL maintenance including structural repairs, which is unusual tenant-side — Section 9.1, p.14. (3) Early termination requires 12 months' notice AND a penalty of 6 months' rent — Section 15.2, p.29. WHAT'S MISSING OR UNCLEAR: The document never specifies who insures the building itself; Section 9 covers contents only. 'Common areas' is used in Sections 6 and 9 but never defined — unclear whether the parking area is included."

A two-minute spot-check of Section 15.2 confirms the penalty claim word for word.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, upload a long document from your actual work or life (a contract, insurance policy, annual report, or lengthy guide) and run the prompt. Then verify two claims from the summary by asking for exact quotes and checking them against the document.
lessons.expectedResult: A one-page brief with cited sections, at least one genuinely useful item in 'missing or unclear', and both of your spot-checked quotes matching the source document.
commonMistakes: Asking for 'a summary' with no purpose attached. You'll get a neutral abstract that buries the two points you actually needed.
Trusting page citations without ever spot-checking. Citations make verification fast; they are not a substitute for doing it, especially before decisions with money or legal weight.

Uploading a scanned document with unreadable text and not noticing the summary is built on fragments. If the summary seems oddly thin, ask 'Were you able to read the full document? Which pages were unclear?'
Stopping at the summary when the value is in the follow-up. The brief tells you where to dig; the drill-down questions are where decisions get made.
lessons.proTip: For contracts and policies, add one line to the prompt: 'Then list the 3 questions I should ask the other party before signing.' It converts the summary into a negotiation checklist.

lessons.title: Pull clean, structured data out of messy notes, emails, and transcripts
lessons.summary: Turn unstructured text — email threads, call notes, feedback dumps — into tidy tables you can paste into a spreadsheet, with nothing invented.
lessons.goal: Extract specific fields from messy text into a clean table, with every missing value marked instead of guessed.
lessons.whyItMatters: A huge share of office work is manual re-typing: reading an email thread and filling a CRM, turning interview notes into a candidate scorecard, collecting order details scattered across messages. Claude does this transformation in seconds — if you define the fields precisely and forbid it from filling blanks with plausible guesses. Done right, this is one of the highest time-return skills in the whole course.
steps: Choose messy source text from your real work: a forwarded email thread, meeting notes, a list of customer replies, a transcript.
Define your columns before you prompt. Write down exactly which fields you need and what format each should have (dates as YYYY-MM-DD, amounts as numbers, etc.).
Paste the prompt below with your field list and the source text. The 'Not stated' rule is the heart of it — keep it.
Check the output row by row against the source for the first run. Pay special attention to any cell that looks suspiciously complete.
Fix systematic errors by refining the field definitions, not by correcting cells one at a time: 'Deadline means the date the CLIENT mentioned, not the date of the email.'
Paste the final table into your spreadsheet or tool. For recurring extractions, save the prompt with your finalized column definitions.
lessons.prompt:
Extract structured data from the text below.

Create one row per [UNIT, e.g. "customer inquiry"] with exactly these columns:
- [FIELD 1, e.g. "Name"]
- [FIELD 2, e.g. "Company"]
- [FIELD 3, e.g. "Request (max 10 words)"]
- [FIELD 4, e.g. "Budget mentioned (number only, or Not stated)"]
- [FIELD 5, e.g. "Deadline (YYYY-MM-DD, or Not stated)"]
- [FIELD 6, e.g. "Urgency: high / medium / low — based only on explicit wording"]

Rules:
- Use ONLY information explicitly present in the text. If a field isn't stated, write exactly "Not stated" — never infer or invent a value.
- If a value is ambiguous, put your best reading followed by "(?)" so I can check it.
- Output as a markdown table, one row per [UNIT], in the order they appear.
- After the table, list anything important in the text that didn't fit the columns.

Text:
[PASTE MESSY TEXT]
lessons.explanation: Precise column definitions do most of the work — 'Budget (number only, or Not stated)' leaves no room for prose answers or currency confusion. The explicit 'Not stated' rule targets the classic failure mode of AI extraction: language models are completion machines, and an empty cell invites a plausible-looking guess; giving them a designated way to say 'nothing here' removes that pressure. The '(?)' convention creates a third category between certain and absent, so ambiguity becomes visible instead of silently resolved. The final 'anything that didn't fit' catch prevents rigid columns from making you blind to the one crucial detail your schema didn't anticipate.
lessons.example:
Input (excerpt of a messy inbox dump): "Fwd: Hi, Elena Marku here from Nordwind Cafe — we talked at the trade fair. We'd want the espresso machine serviced before we reopen March 14, budget's tight, maybe 300? … Second mail: George from Alpha Catering, need a full quote for 2 machines + grinder, no rush, sometime next quarter is fine …"

Output: A table with rows | Elena Marku | Nordwind Cafe | Espresso machine service | 300 (?) | 2026-03-14 | high | and | George [surname Not stated] | Alpha Catering | Quote: 2 machines + grinder | Not stated | Not stated | low |, followed by: "Note outside the columns: Elena references meeting you at a trade fair — possibly relevant for the follow-up's opening line. Her budget is phrased as a question ('maybe 300?'), hence the (?)."
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, paste 5-10 real unstructured items (emails, notes, or feedback snippets), define 4-6 columns for what you'd want in a spreadsheet, and run the prompt. Verify every 'Not stated' and every '(?)' against the source.
lessons.expectedResult: A clean table you could paste into Excel or a CRM, where filled cells trace back to explicit text, gaps say 'Not stated', and ambiguous readings are flagged rather than hidden.
commonMistakes: Vague field names. 'Status' means nothing; 'Status: replied / awaiting reply / closed — based on the last message in the thread' produces consistent results.
Omitting the 'Not stated' rule and getting a beautifully complete table where a third of the values are invented. Complete-looking is not the same as correct.
Extracting 200 items in one giant paste and reviewing none of them. Run a small batch first, verify, refine the prompt, then scale up.
Correcting individual cells by hand each time instead of fixing the field definition — the same error will return on every future run.
lessons.proTip: Ask for the output 'as CSV in a code block' instead of a markdown table when you're heading to a spreadsheet — it pastes cleanly into Excel or Google Sheets via 'split text to columns'.

lessons.title: Turn rough bullet points into polished professional emails
lessons.summary: Go from five messy bullets to a send-ready email in under two minutes — matched to the reader, the relationship, and the outcome you want.
lessons.goal: Draft professional emails from quick bullet points, so the thinking stays yours and the wording takes seconds.
lessons.whyItMatters: You already know what the email needs to say — the twenty minutes go into phrasing, ordering, and tone-calibrating, especially for delicate messages: declining work, chasing payment, delivering bad news. Splitting the job (you supply the substance as bullets, Claude supplies the prose) is faster than writing from scratch and safer than letting AI decide what to say. This is the single most-used AI skill in most professionals' week.
steps: Before opening Claude, jot your bullets: every point the email must make, in any order, as fragments. Include the awkward ones — 'need to say no without killing future work'.
Note three facts about the send: who the reader is, what your relationship is, and what you want to happen after they read it.
Paste the prompt below. Ask for two versions when tone is tricky — choosing between drafts is easier than describing perfect tone upfront.
Read the draft aloud (or subvocalize). Anywhere it doesn't sound like you, tell Claude specifically: 'I'd never say I hope this finds you well — cut openers like that.'
Check that every bullet made it in and nothing was added — especially commitments, dates, or apologies you didn't ask for.
Copy into your email client, give it one final human read, and send.
lessons.prompt:
Write an email from my bullet points.

To: [WHO — role and your relationship, e.g. "client of 3 years, friendly but professional"]
Goal: after reading, they should [DESIRED ACTION OR FEELING]
Tone: [e.g. "warm but direct; apologetic about the delay without groveling"]
Length: [e.g. "under 150 words"]

My points (all must be included; add nothing substantive I haven't listed — no new commitments, offers, or reasons):
- [BULLET 1]
- [BULLET 2]
- [BULLET 3]
- [BULLET 4]

Give me 2 versions: one safer/more formal, one warmer/more direct. Then a subject line for each.
lessons.explanation: The bullets keep authorship where it belongs — every substantive point is yours, so the email can't commit you to anything you didn't decide. The 'add nothing substantive' rule matters more than it looks: helpful models love to append 'happy to jump on a call!' or an extra concession that changes your negotiating position. Reader, relationship, and goal give Claude what it needs to calibrate register (the same content reads very differently to a new prospect versus a three-year client). Two versions exploit a general truth about working with AI: humans are far better at picking the right tone from options than at specifying it in advance.
lessons.example:
Input bullets: "- can't take their April project, fully booked
- genuinely want to work with them later
- can recommend Dana Petrou for this one
- ask them to keep me in mind for Q3". To: "marketing manager at a company I've wanted as a client for a year; we've met twice." Goal: "decline without closing the door."

Output (warmer version): "Subject: April timing — and an alternative. Hi Sofia, Thank you for thinking of me for the April campaign — I'd genuinely like to work together, which makes this harder to write: I'm fully committed through April and couldn't give it the attention it deserves. If timing is flexible, I'd love to talk about Q3. If it isn't, Dana Petrou (copied-style intro available on request) does excellent work in exactly this space. Either way, I hope this is the start rather than the end of the conversation. — Alex"
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, take a real email you need to send this week, write it first as 3-6 bullets, and run the prompt. Send the version you'd actually stand behind — after checking every bullet arrived and nothing new appeared.
lessons.expectedResult: A send-ready email in your chosen tone, produced in under two minutes, containing all of your points and zero commitments you didn't make.
commonMistakes: Giving Claude the topic instead of the points ('write an email declining a project'). Now the AI is deciding your reasons and concessions — that's backwards.
Skipping the relationship description. 'Client' spans everything from a stranger to a friend of a decade; the tone calibration depends entirely on which.
Sending without the final human read. You are responsible for every word; two minutes of review is the price of putting your name on it.
Letting drafts grow. If your bullets fit in 100 words, a 300-word email is padding — enforce the length limit.
lessons.proTip: For email threads, paste the whole thread above your bullets and add 'Reply to the last message in this thread.' Claude will pick up names, open questions, and the register the conversation is already in.

lessons.title: Get to a great answer faster with follow-ups instead of restarts
lessons.summary: Learn the five follow-up moves that turn an okay first draft into an excellent final one — and when a fresh chat really is the better call.
lessons.goal: Steer a conversation from a mediocre first response to a strong final result using targeted follow-ups, without re-explaining anything.
lessons.whyItMatters: Beginners treat every Claude response as a verdict: if it's not right, they rewrite the prompt from scratch in a new chat, losing all accumulated context. Experienced users treat the first response as a first draft and spend their effort on follow-ups — which are cheap, fast, and compound, because Claude remembers everything already established in the conversation. The difference in output quality between one-shot users and iterative users is enormous, and the technique takes ten minutes to learn.
steps: Start any real task (use a prompt from an earlier lesson). Read the first response as a draft to direct, not a result to accept or reject.
Move 1 — Adjust one dial: change a single dimension and name it. 'Same structure, but half the length.' 'Keep everything, just make the tone less formal.'
Move 2 — Point at the part: reference the exact section instead of critiquing the whole. 'Paragraph 2 is generic — replace it with something specific to the retail context I described.'
Move 3 — Ask for variations: 'Give me 3 alternative versions of just the opening line, ranging from safe to bold.' Then pick, rather than describe.
Move 4 — Make Claude the critic: 'Before I use this, critique it: what's weakest, what would a skeptical reader push back on?' Then: 'Fix those issues.'
Move 5 — Add the context you forgot: new information doesn't need a restart. 'I forgot to mention the deadline is Friday — rework the plan around that.'

Know when to actually restart: if the chat is littered with abandoned directions and Claude keeps resurrecting ideas you've rejected, open a fresh chat and paste in only the good final pieces plus your original context.
lessons.prompt:
Before I use your draft, do a critique pass on it:
1. What are the 2-3 weakest parts, and why?
2. What would a skeptical [READER, e.g. "CFO" / "experienced buyer"] push back on or distrust?
3. What did I ask for that you didn't fully deliver?

Be specific — point at exact sentences or sections. Don't rewrite anything yet; just critique.
lessons.explanation: Follow-ups work because the conversation is state: everything you've established — context, constraints, rejected directions — stays in play, so a six-word follow-up ('half the length, keep the table') carries all of it forward. Adjusting one dial at a time makes cause and effect visible; changing three things at once means you can't tell which change helped. The self-critique move is the most underused: Claude is genuinely better at finding flaws when asked to critique than it is at spontaneously avoiding them, and separating 'critique' from 'fix' stops it from rubber-stamping its own work. The restart rule exists because very long, contradiction-filled chats can degrade — the fix is a clean chat seeded with only the surviving good material.
lessons.example:
Turn 1: A product description for a handmade furniture shop — decent but generic. Turn 2 (adjust one dial): "Half the length, keep the wood-sourcing detail." Better, still flat. Turn 3 (point at the part): "The first sentence could describe any furniture store. Rewrite just that sentence, using the fact that every piece is built to order in our own workshop." Turn 4 (variations): "3 versions of that sentence, safe to bold." Turn 5 (critique): "What would a skeptical buyer distrust here?" — Claude flags the unsupported 'heirloom quality' claim. Turn 6: "Fair. Replace it with the 10-year guarantee, which is real."

Final result: five short follow-ups, no restarts, and a description that survives skeptical reading — total time about six minutes.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, take any writing task and deliberately practice the moves: get a first draft, then use at least three different follow-up moves from the steps (including the self-critique prompt) before you accept the result.
lessons.expectedResult: A final version noticeably stronger than the first draft, reached through short targeted follow-ups — and a feel for how little text each follow-up actually needs.
commonMistakes: Restarting in a new chat after every imperfect answer, re-typing context each time. Iteration in-place is faster and compounds.
Vague dissatisfaction: 'that's not quite right, try again' gives Claude nothing to steer by. Name what's wrong and where.
Changing everything at once ('shorter, funnier, more formal, restructured') — you lose track of what worked.
Iterating past the peak. When two consecutive versions aren't improving, stop — pick the best one and finish it by hand.
lessons.proTip: When a response is 90% right, don't ask for a revision — ask for the delta: 'Keep everything exactly as is, except replace the third bullet.' Full regenerations sometimes churn parts you'd already approved.

lessons.title: Set up a Claude Project so every chat starts already knowing your work
lessons.summary: Stop re-explaining your business in every conversation: put your context, documents, and standing instructions into a Claude Project once.
lessons.goal: Create a Claude Project with custom instructions and knowledge files, so new chats start with your full working context already loaded.
lessons.whyItMatters: By this point in the course you've noticed the pattern: the quality of Claude's output tracks the quality of context you provide — and you keep typing the same context. Projects fix that. A Project is a workspace where you upload reference files and write standing instructions once; every chat inside it starts with all of it. For anyone who uses Claude for the same client, product, or role every day, this is the single biggest quality-per-keystroke upgrade in the app.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Projects require a paid plan (Pro, from $20/month, or higher). On Free, you can still apply the idea manually: keep a 'context block' text file and paste it at the top of important chats.
steps: In the claude.ai sidebar, open Projects and create a new one. Name it for one stream of work — 'Acme Corp — Marketing' or 'My Freelance Business' — not 'Everything'.
Write the custom instructions using the template below: who you are, what this project covers, and standing rules for how Claude should respond.
Add knowledge files: the 3-10 documents that recur in your prompts — brand or style guide, price list, service descriptions, key client briefs, a good example of your output.
Start a chat inside the project and test with a deliberately short prompt like 'Draft a follow-up email for the Meridian offer.' If the project is set up well, the short prompt now works.
Fix gaps at the source: when a chat reveals missing context, add it to the project instructions or files — not just to that chat — so every future chat benefits.
Create separate projects for genuinely separate streams (one per major client or function), so unrelated context never bleeds together.
lessons.prompt:
ABOUT ME / THIS PROJECT:
I am [ROLE] at [BUSINESS — one line on what it does and for whom]. This project is for [THE STREAM OF WORK, e.g. "all client-facing writing for my consulting practice"].

STANDING CONTEXT:
- [KEY FACT 1, e.g. "My clients are small manufacturers, 10-100 employees, non-technical"]
- [KEY FACT 2, e.g. "Prices: audit 1,500 EUR; monthly retainer 800 EUR — never discount in writing"]
- [KEY FACT 3]

HOW TO RESPOND IN THIS PROJECT:
- Tone: [e.g. "plain, direct, warm; no hype words like game-changing or unlock"]
- Language/format defaults: [e.g. "emails under 150 words; UK English; dates as 14 March"]
- Use the knowledge files as the source of truth about my business. If they don't cover something, ask me — do not invent details about my services, prices, or clients.
- [ANY HARD RULE, e.g. "Never promise delivery dates without me stating one"]
lessons.explanation: Project instructions are lesson 2's context-role-constraints structure made permanent: written once, applied to every chat automatically. The 'source of truth' line is the key guardrail — it tells Claude that your uploaded files outrank its general knowledge, and that gaps should produce questions rather than plausible inventions about your prices or services. Scoping each project narrowly keeps the context truthful for every chat inside it (a project that covers everything is accurate for nothing). And the maintenance habit in step 5 is what makes projects improve over time: every gap you discover once, you fix for all future chats.
lessons.example:
Before: every Monday, a consultant types 200 words of context ('I run a safety-compliance consultancy for food manufacturers, my tone is plain and direct, our audit costs 1,500 EUR...') before asking for each proposal or follow-up email.

After: her 'Consultancy — Client Writing' project contains those instructions plus five files: service descriptions, price list, two winning past proposals, and a tone guide. Monday's entire prompt is now: 'Draft a proposal for Delta Foods — dairy plant, 40 staff, failed their last hygiene audit, want the full package.' The output arrives in her tone, with correct prices, structured like her winning proposals — because the project supplied everything the old 200-word preamble used to, plus more.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account (paid plan), create one project for your most repetitive stream of work: write instructions from the template and upload at least three real reference files. Then test it with a one-sentence prompt that would have failed without the project.
lessons.expectedResult: The one-sentence prompt produces output that reflects your tone, your facts, and your formats. If it doesn't, identify what was missing and add it to the project — then the same short prompt should succeed.
commonMistakes: One giant project for everything. Mixed contexts produce mixed-up outputs — Claude can't tell which client's tone or prices apply. One project per stream of work.
Uploading 40 files 'just in case'. Curate: a few high-signal documents beat a dump of stale ones, and outdated files actively mislead.
Writing instructions once and never updating them. Prices change, services change; a project with stale facts confidently produces stale outputs.
Fixing recurring problems chat by chat instead of in the project. If you've corrected the same thing twice, it belongs in the instructions.
lessons.proTip: Add one file called 'gold-standard-examples' containing 2-3 of your best past outputs (a proposal that won, an email that landed). 'Match the style of the gold-standard examples' outperforms any abstract tone description.

lessons.title: Upload a spreadsheet and get a plain-language readout of what it says
lessons.summary: Hand Claude a CSV or Excel file and get the story in the numbers — trends, outliers, and answers to specific questions — without writing a single formula.
lessons.goal: Upload a data file and extract a trustworthy plain-language readout: what's in it, what stands out, and answers to your specific business questions.
lessons.whyItMatters: Most professionals sit on spreadsheets they never fully read: sales exports, expense reports, survey results, booking logs. The blocker isn't the data — it's that interrogating it requires formulas, pivot tables, or a colleague who knows them. Claude removes that blocker: it can read your file, run real calculations on it using its built-in analysis tool, and explain findings in sentences. Your job shifts from computing answers to asking good questions and sanity-checking what comes back.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have a real CSV or Excel file with at least a few dozen rows. Remove or anonymize columns you shouldn't share externally (names, emails) — for most analyses, Claude doesn't need them.
steps: Upload the file via the attachment icon and send the prompt below. The first pass is deliberately about orientation, not conclusions.

Read the orientation summary and correct any misreadings immediately: 'Column D is order value in EUR including VAT, not profit.' Everything downstream depends on Claude reading the columns correctly.
Ask your real business questions one at a time, in plain language: 'Which product line is growing fastest this year?' 'Which customers haven't ordered in 90+ days?'

For every number that matters, ask how it was computed: 'Show the calculation behind that 23% — which rows and columns went into it?' Claude can run actual code on your data; asking for the method makes results checkable.
Sanity-check at least one key figure against something you know independently (last month's total revenue, headcount, a number from your accounting tool).
Ask for the wrap-up: 'Summarize the 3 most decision-relevant findings in plain language, each with the number that supports it.' Paste that into your notes or team update.
lessons.prompt:
I've uploaded [WHAT THE FILE IS, e.g. "a CSV export of all 2025 orders from my online shop"]. Context: [ONE OR TWO SENTENCES — what the business is, what a row represents, anything odd about the data].

Start with orientation only — no conclusions yet:
1. What columns does the file contain, and what does each appear to mean? Flag any you're unsure how to interpret.
2. Basic shape: how many rows, what date range, any obvious data-quality issues (duplicates, gaps, weird values)?

Wait for me to confirm your reading of the columns. After that I'll ask questions — when you answer them:
- Compute answers from the actual data (run the analysis, don't estimate)
- Give every answer in plain language first, then the supporting numbers
- Say which columns/rows each calculation used
- If the data can't answer a question, say so — don't approximate silently
lessons.explanation: The two-phase structure is the safety mechanism: most bad data analyses fail at the reading stage (a mislabeled column, VAT-inclusive figures treated as profit), so the prompt forces a confirm-the-columns checkpoint before any conclusions exist. 'Run the analysis, don't estimate' matters because Claude can execute real code against your file — you want computed answers, not impressions from skimming rows. Asking for the method behind each number gives you the same auditability a formula bar gives a spreadsheet. And the independent sanity check in step 5 is non-negotiable professional hygiene: one figure verified against a source you trust validates the whole pipeline.
lessons.example:
Input: orders-2025.csv (1,847 rows) from a small online cookware shop, plus the orientation prompt.

Orientation output: "8 columns: order_date, customer_id, product, category, quantity, unit_price, discount_pct, region. 1,847 rows spanning 2025-01-02 to 2025-12-30. Data-quality flags: 12 rows have quantity 0; region is blank for 89 rows; there are two 'Pans' spellings ('Pans', 'pans ') that likely need merging."

After confirming columns, the question "Which category drives revenue, and is anything declining?" returns: "Cast iron drives 41% of revenue (34,120 EUR of 83,220 EUR total, computed as quantity x unit_price x (1 - discount_pct) summed by category). One decline stands out: bakeware revenue fell every quarter, from 6,410 EUR in Q1 to 3,180 EUR in Q4 — a 50% drop, driven by falling order counts, not smaller orders." The shop owner checks total 2025 revenue against her accounting software: it matches within rounding.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, upload a real data file from your work (sales export, expenses, survey results — anonymized as needed). Run the orientation prompt, correct at least one column interpretation, ask three business questions, and verify one key figure against an independent source.
lessons.expectedResult: A plain-language readout with three concrete findings you didn't have before, each backed by a stated calculation — and one figure cross-checked successfully against a source outside Claude.
commonMistakes: Skipping orientation and jumping straight to 'what are the insights?' — misread columns produce fluent, confident, wrong analysis.
Accepting percentages without asking for the method. 'Revenue grew 23%' means nothing until you know 23% of what, over what period, computed how.
Never sanity-checking against an external number. One two-minute cross-check is the difference between analysis and vibes.
Uploading a file whose data-quality problems (duplicates, test rows, mixed currencies) you know about but don't mention. Tell Claude what you know is dirty; it will handle it explicitly.
lessons.proTip: End data sessions with: 'What question SHOULD I be asking about this data that I haven't?' — on real business files this reliably surfaces one angle (seasonality, concentration risk, a quiet decline) you hadn't considered.

lessons.title: Research with Claude's web search — and verify before you rely on it
lessons.summary: Use Claude's built-in web search for current information and brainstorming grounded in reality — with the verification habits that keep you from repeating someone else's mistake.
lessons.goal: Run a real research task with Claude's web search, get a cited summary, and verify the claims that matter before acting on them.
lessons.whyItMatters: Claude's built-in knowledge has a cutoff and doesn't include today's prices, this year's regulations, or your competitor's current offer. Web search fixes that: Claude searches the live web, reads sources, and synthesizes an answer with citations. But synthesis is not verification — a fluent summary of five sources can still repeat one source's error. Professionals who use AI research well share one habit: they click through on the claims that carry weight. This lesson builds that habit in.
steps: Pick a research question where currency matters: market rates for a service, recent regulation changes, comparing current tools or suppliers, what competitors are doing now.
Send the prompt below. Explicitly asking Claude to search matters when recency is critical — it makes the live search happen rather than leaving it to Claude's judgment.
Read the answer with the citations visible. Notice which claims have sources attached and which are Claude's own synthesis or inference.

Apply the two-source rule to load-bearing claims: for any fact you'll act on (a price, a deadline, a legal requirement), open the cited source and confirm it says what the summary says — and check the date.
Interrogate disagreement: 'Did the sources disagree on anything? What did each say?' Real research questions rarely have unanimous sources; surfacing the spread is more honest than averaging it away.
For brainstorming tasks, run search-grounded ideation: 'Search for how businesses like mine handle X, then propose 5 approaches — noting which are common practice and which are your own suggestions.'
lessons.prompt:
Research this for me using web search: [YOUR QUESTION, e.g. "What do freelance UX designers in Germany currently charge per day, as of this year?"]

Context for relevance: [WHY YOU'RE ASKING, e.g. "I'm setting my 2026 rates; 6 years of experience, mostly B2B software clients"]

Requirements:
- Search for current information; my question is time-sensitive
- Cite sources for every factual claim, and include the date of the information where you can find it
- Clearly separate three things: (a) facts from sources, (b) where sources disagree — show the range, don't average it — and (c) your own inference or advice, labeled as such
- If you can't find solid current information on some part, say exactly that — an honest gap beats a stale or shaky number

End with: the 2-3 claims in your answer I should verify myself before acting, and why those in particular.
lessons.explanation: The three-way separation — sourced fact, source disagreement, Claude's inference — is the heart of this prompt: most research answers blur these into one confident voice, and un-blurring them is what makes the answer auditable. Showing ranges instead of averages respects how real-world data actually looks (rates, prices, and timelines are spreads, not points). The closing request flips verification from your job to a shared one: Claude is well positioned to know which of its claims are load-bearing and least certain, and asking it to nominate them gives you a two-item checklist instead of a vague duty to 'double-check everything'. The honest-gap rule counters the strongest failure pressure in AI research: the pull to produce a complete-sounding answer whether or not the sources support one.
lessons.example:
Input: the rates question above, asked by a freelance UX designer.

Output (structure): "FROM SOURCES: Freelance platform surveys and rate reports put German freelance UX day rates at roughly 550-950 EUR depending on seniority and industry [citations with dates]. WHERE SOURCES DISAGREE: one 2026 rate survey centers on ~700 EUR/day; a freelancer-platform report skews lower (~600), likely because platform rates undercut direct-client rates — I'm showing the spread rather than averaging. MY INFERENCE (not sourced): with 6 years and B2B software focus, the upper-middle of the range (750-850) is defensible with direct clients. VERIFY YOURSELF: (1) the 700 EUR survey figure — it's the newest but from a single source; (2) whether rates in your city differ materially from the national figures, which none of my sources broke down."

The designer clicks the survey link, confirms the figure and its date, and sets rates with evidence rather than a guess.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, research a question from your real work where being current matters. Use the prompt, then actually perform the verification step: open at least two cited sources and confirm the claims Claude flagged for checking.
lessons.expectedResult: A cited, honestly-structured research summary — and at least one moment where clicking through taught you something the summary compressed away (a date, a caveat, a disagreement). That moment is the habit forming.
commonMistakes: Treating a cited answer as a verified answer. Citations make checking possible; they don't make it done. Click through on anything you'll act on.
Not checking source dates. A confidently cited 2023 figure answering a 'current rates' question is the most common silent failure in AI research.
Asking for 'the answer' when the truth is a range. If you force a single number, you get false precision; ask for the spread and where you sit in it.

Using web search for things Claude knows timelessly (how to structure a proposal, general how-tos) — you'll get slower answers assembled from mediocre articles instead of Claude's own stronger synthesis. Search is for facts that change.
lessons.proTip: For competitive research, name the entities: 'Search for the current pricing pages of [Competitor A] and [Competitor B] specifically, and build a comparison table with a source link per row.' Naming targets beats hoping the right ones surface.

lessons.title: Build reusable prompt templates for the tasks you repeat every week
lessons.summary: Turn your best one-off prompts into a personal template library with fill-in placeholders — so recurring tasks take one paste instead of fresh prompt-writing.
lessons.goal: Create at least two tested, placeholder-based prompt templates for your recurring tasks and store them where you can reuse them in seconds.
lessons.whyItMatters: By now you've written good prompts — and if you're like most users, you've also lost them in your chat history and rebuilt them from memory, slightly worse, the next week. A prompt that took ten minutes to refine is an asset. Templating it — placeholders for what changes, refined wording for what doesn't — turns your best prompting into infrastructure: consistent quality, zero setup time, and something you can hand to a colleague. This is how individual AI skill becomes a repeatable workflow.
steps: List your recurring Claude tasks: anything you've prompted for twice. Typical candidates: weekly client updates, meeting-notes-to-actions, proposal sections, review responses, job-ad drafts.
Pick the most frequent one and find your best past attempt in your chat history — including the follow-up corrections you made, which encode what the first version got wrong.
Use the prompt below to have Claude build the template with you: it separates what varies per use (placeholders) from what should be permanent (your refined instructions, tone, guardrails).
Test the template immediately on a real instance of the task. Fix weaknesses in the TEMPLATE text, not in the chat — the template is the product here.

Store templates somewhere with two-click access: a notes app, a text file, or a doc titled 'Claude templates'. Name each by task ('Weekly status update — client'), and add a one-line 'when to use this'.
Repeat for your second most frequent task. Two solid templates in week one beats ten untested ones.
Maintain like code: every time a template's output needs the same correction twice, edit the template so the correction is permanent.
lessons.prompt:
Help me turn a task I do repeatedly into a reusable prompt template.

The recurring task: [DESCRIBE IT, e.g. "every Friday I write a status update email to each active client about their project"]

Here is a prompt (or conversation) that worked well for one instance of it, including my corrections:
[PASTE YOUR BEST PAST PROMPT AND ANY FOLLOW-UP FIXES]

Build me a template:
1. Replace everything instance-specific with CAPITALIZED placeholders in brackets, each with a short hint, e.g. [CLIENT NAME], [WHAT SHIPPED THIS WEEK - bullets], [BLOCKERS - or "none"]
2. Make everything that should be constant permanent in the template: tone, format, length limits, and guardrails (e.g. "include nothing not listed in the bullets")
3. Bake my past corrections into the standing instructions so I never have to repeat them
4. Keep it as short as it can be while still producing consistent results
5. End with a 'HOW TO USE' line: which placeholders to fill and any tip for filling them well
lessons.explanation: The key design question of any template is which parts vary and which don't — placeholders for the first, permanently refined wording for the second. Building from your best past conversation (not from scratch) matters because your follow-up corrections are compressed knowledge: each one marks a spot where the naive prompt failed, and step 3 bakes those fixes in so they're made once, forever. Using Claude to build the template is itself the meta-skill — it's good at spotting which parts of a prompt were instance-specific. Testing on a real task before storing is what separates a template library from a folder of plausible-looking prompts that fail on contact.
lessons.example:
Input: a marketing freelancer's best Friday-update prompt, plus her two recurring corrections ('never say issues, say what we're watching' and 'always end with next week's top priority').

Output template (condensed): "Write my weekly status email for [CLIENT NAME], project [PROJECT]. This week's completed work: [SHIPPED - bullets]. In progress: [IN PROGRESS - bullets]. Concerns: [WATCHING - bullets, or 'none']. Rules: under 150 words; confident but honest tone; frame concerns as 'what we're watching', never 'issues'; include nothing not in my bullets; always end with next week's single top priority: [TOP PRIORITY]. HOW TO USE: fill the four bullet placeholders from your task tracker; write WATCHING honestly — the framing rule handles the diplomacy."

Her Friday updates now take 3 minutes each, and all clients get the same consistent quality — including the two rules she used to re-explain weekly.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, build and test templates for your two most frequent recurring tasks using the template-builder prompt. Store both in your notes tool with names and 'when to use' lines, then use one for real this week.
lessons.expectedResult: Two stored templates that produce reliable output from just filled placeholders — and a real task this week completed noticeably faster because the prompt already existed.
commonMistakes: Templating a task you've only done once. Templates encode learning; with one data point there's nothing to encode. Prompt freely first, template on repetition.
Placeholders without hints. Future-you will fill [DETAILS] lazily; [WHAT SHIPPED THIS WEEK - 2-5 bullets, specific] extracts the right input.
Storing templates in chat history. Chats scroll away; templates live in a place with a name and two-click access.
Letting templates rot. If you're correcting the same output flaw repeatedly, the fix belongs in the template — that maintenance habit is the whole point.
lessons.proTip: If you're on a paid plan, pair this with lesson 8: put a template's permanent instructions into a Project's custom instructions, and the 'template' you paste per-use shrinks to just the filled placeholders.

lessons.title: Design your personal Claude workflow: habits, defaults, and the right plan
lessons.summary: Turn eleven lessons of techniques into a durable daily workflow: decide where Claude fits in your week, set up your environment, and choose the plan that matches your usage.
lessons.goal: Leave with a written personal workflow: your top recurring Claude use cases, the setup that supports them, and a deliberate plan choice.
lessons.whyItMatters: Skills fade without structure. The people who still use AI effectively a year after learning it aren't the ones who learned the most techniques — they're the ones who wired a few techniques into their actual week: default tasks that always go through Claude, templates ready to paste, a Project per work stream. This closing lesson is deliberately practical: audit your week, install the habits, and make an informed decision about what plan (if any) to pay for.
steps: Run the workflow-audit prompt below. It uses everything this course taught to analyze your own week and propose where Claude genuinely fits — and where it doesn't.

From the output, choose your top 3 'default to Claude' tasks: recurring work where the course showed clear time savings (drafting from bullets, document summaries, data readouts, rewrites). Write them down — a visible list, not a mental note.

Set up your environment for those three: the templates from lesson 11 stored and named, a Project (lesson 8) if you're on a paid plan, the claude.ai desktop and mobile apps installed so Claude is one click away, memory settings reviewed in Settings so context carries across chats the way you want.

Choose your plan deliberately. Free: fine for light, occasional use — limited usage per session. Pro ($20/month, less on annual): removes the main limits and unlocks the features this course used — Projects, the model picker, and higher usage per 5-hour session window. Max tiers ($100-$200/month): for heavy daily users who hit Pro's limits; more capacity per session window. Match the plan to your audit, not to enthusiasm.

Learn your usage rhythm: Claude plans meter usage in rolling 5-hour session windows plus weekly caps. If you hit a limit mid-task, it resets with the window — plan heavy sessions accordingly rather than assuming something broke.

Install one weekly habit: a 10-minute Friday review — which tasks went through Claude, which templates need fixing, what you re-explained twice that belongs in a Project. This is the maintenance loop that keeps the whole system improving.
Write the one-page workflow doc: your 3 default tasks, where your templates live, your projects, your plan, and your review day. That page is this course's real deliverable.
lessons.prompt:
Help me design my personal AI workflow. I've completed a beginner course on you (Claude) covering: structured prompting, rewriting drafts, summarizing documents, extracting structured data, drafting emails from bullets, iterating with follow-ups, Projects, spreadsheet analysis, web research with verification, and prompt templates.

My typical work week: [DESCRIBE HONESTLY — your role, the 6-10 tasks that eat most of your time, roughly how many hours each, which you find draining]

Give me:
1. The 3 tasks from my week where Claude will save the most time — for each: which technique applies, the realistic time saving per week, and a one-line starter prompt
2. 1-2 tasks from my list where Claude is a POOR fit and I should not force it — with the reason
3. A concrete first-week plan: what to set up (templates, a Project?) and in what order, assuming 30 minutes of setup time total
4. Based on the volume you see in my week: is the Free plan enough for this, or does Pro pay for itself? Show your reasoning against my actual task volume — don't assume upgrading is the answer.

Be honest and specific. If parts of my week are bad AI use cases, I want to know that clearly.
lessons.explanation: The audit prompt applies the course to its own subject: your context (the honest week description) is the input, and the output is scoped by constraints that force honesty — naming poor fits, and justifying the plan recommendation against your actual volume instead of defaulting to 'upgrade'. Asking for realistic time savings per task keeps the plan grounded; asking for a 30-minute setup sequence converts advice into something you'll actually do this week. The Friday review habit in the steps is the compounding mechanism: templates get fixed, Projects absorb repeated context, and your three default tasks stay genuinely default. The written one-pager matters because workflows that exist only as intentions dissolve within a month.
lessons.example:
Input: "I'm an operations manager at a 30-person logistics company. Week: staff scheduling (4h), replying to customer emails (6h), weekly management report (3h), analyzing delivery-performance exports (2h), supplier calls (3h), incident write-ups (2h). Most draining: the report and the incident write-ups."

Output (condensed): "Top 3: (1) Weekly management report — bullets-to-draft plus your data-readout technique on the delivery export; realistic saving ~2h/week; starter: 'Draft my weekly ops report from these bullets and the attached export...'. (2) Customer email replies — template per common scenario (delay, damage claim, quote); ~2h/week. (3) Incident write-ups — structured extraction from your raw notes into your incident format; ~1h/week. POOR FIT: supplier calls — relationship work, use Claude only for pre-call prep; staff scheduling — a constraints problem your scheduling tool handles better than a chat. FIRST WEEK: build the report template Monday (15 min), one email template Wednesday (10 min), skip Projects until the templates stabilize. PLAN: your ~5h/week of drafting and one data analysis fits comfortably in Pro; you'd likely hit Free's session limits on report day alone — Pro pays for itself if it saves even 20 minutes/week at your hourly cost."
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, run the workflow audit with an honest description of your real week. Then complete the first-week plan it gives you: set up at least one template or Project, and put a 10-minute review in your calendar for Friday.
lessons.expectedResult: A written one-page workflow — 3 default tasks, setup done for at least one of them, a deliberate plan decision, and a recurring review slot in your calendar. If you can show someone that page, the course did its job.
commonMistakes: Trying to route everything through Claude. Forced use cases fail, and the failures erode trust in the good ones. Three solid defaults beat ten shaky ones.
Upgrading plans based on excitement rather than hitting actual limits. Let the Free or Pro limits tell you when you've outgrown them — the audit's volume reasoning is the guide.
Skipping the written workflow doc. Intentions decay in weeks; a one-pager plus a calendar slot survives.

Treating this course as finished knowledge. The tool gains features regularly (and paid plans add more, like Skills and file-creating capabilities you'll meet in intermediate lessons) — the Friday review is also where you notice what's new.
lessons.proTip: Reviews go better with data: Claude's memory means you can ask it directly — 'Based on our conversations these past weeks, what am I using you for most, and where do my prompts tend to be weakest?' Your own usage becomes the input for improving it.
